> 寵辱若驚，貴大患若身.

Chapter 3 removed the external standards: don't honor talent, don't price rare goods, don't display the desirable. Chapter 13 takes one step inward and asks the question that chapter 3 left open.

The standards are gone. Who is still chasing them?

The answer is the 我 — the self that handed itself over. Favor and disgrace can shake a person not because they have power, but because the person has already deposited the verdict about himself in someone else's mouth.

## 寵為下

> 何謂寵辱若驚？寵為下，得之若驚，失之若驚.

The striking move is 寵為下: favor is the lower position.

Receiving favor puts you in a relation where the giver is above and the gift is a mark. The one who is favored is now holding something that can be withdrawn. So 得之若驚 and 失之若驚 are the same disturbance: the favor itself is the instability, not only its loss.

This is why the chapter does not contrast favor with disgrace as good versus bad. Both are events in the same vertical relation, and both keep you oriented upward.

## 大患的落點

> 吾所以有大患者，為吾有身；及吾無身，吾有何患？

The 身 here is not the body as a physical object. It is the self treated as a boundary — the "me" that has to be protected, defended, and kept consistent.

As long as that boundary is treated as the thing that must not be touched, every event in the world is a potential threat. The worry is not caused by events; it is caused by the maintenance of the boundary.

## 無身 is not self-destruction

This is the line that gets read as world-weariness or self-erasure. It is neither.

無身 does not mean "get rid of the body." It means: don't nail the 我 onto that boundary. The body remains; the self remains as a functioning center; what is dropped is the assumption that the boundary is what you are.

There is a testable difference. With the boundary treated as yourself, criticism is a physical event and rest is impossible. With the boundary treated as a position you occupy, criticism is information about the position, and rest is available.

## 貴以身為天下

> 故貴以身為天下，若可寄天下；愛以身為天下，若可托天下.

The last line looks like a political criterion: the one who values his body as he values the world can be entrusted with the world.

Read alongside 無身, it is not a contradiction. The person who can be trusted with power is the one whose self is not the thing being defended at all costs — because such a person can absorb a cost without converting it into a personal wound, and can act on what the situation requires rather than on what protects the boundary.

The person who treats the self as a boundary will treat the world as a resource for defending it. That is the failure mode of most leadership, and it is what the line is guarding against.

## The two chapters together

Chapter 3 removes the ruler outside; chapter 13 removes the ruler inside. Neither is sufficient alone: with only the external removed, the self keeps manufacturing standards and then obeying them; with only the internal removed, external standards still flow in unexamined.

Together they describe the same operation from two sides: stop handing the verdict to something that can take it back.

## A test

Recall the last piece of praise that changed your behavior. Ask what you did differently afterward, and whether you would have done it without the praise. That dependency is the 寵為下 the chapter is talking about.
